hints: Count carbons in A, $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, against the six peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum to decide what symmetry the benzene ring must have.
Use the reaction with excess $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ to identify the functional group that activates the ring, and use the formula change from A to B to count how many ring hydrogens are replaced.
Recall what structural fragment gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, and what happens to the rest of that fragment.
Combine the phenol evidence with the methyl ketone evidence to build A as a disubstituted benzene, then use the 13C peak count to choose between ortho, meta and para isomers.
Track the carbon count from A to D to E: loss of one carbon in the iodoform reaction tells you D is a benzoic acid type, then $\text{PCl}_5$ tells you the functional group change in E.
Recall the product of an acyl chloride plus an alcohol such as propan-2-ol to deduce the functional group in F.
walkthrough:
Work out what A must contain from two classic tests**
Think with me side by side. Decolourising bromine water with white precipitate formation is the signature of a phenol, specifically electrophilic substitution activated by the $\text{-OH}$ group. Forming a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2(aq)$ is the triiodomethane test, positive for a methyl ketone group, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$. So A contains both a phenolic $\text{OH}$ and a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ group attached to a benzene ring. That fits $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$ plus $\text{OH}$ plus $\text{COCH}_3$.

Use the bromination stoichiometry to count free positions**
Look at the formulas: A is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, B is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{Br}_2\text{O}_2$. Two H atoms have been replaced by two Br atoms. With excess bromine water a phenol substitutes at all available ortho and para positions to $\text{OH}$. Getting a dibromo product means exactly two positions were free. That happens when the para position to $\text{OH}$ is already occupied by the other substituent, leaving the two ortho positions free.

Use the 13C NMR to prove para substitution**
A has 8 carbons but only six peaks in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR. A benzene with two different substituents has 2 side chain carbons ($\text{C=O}$ and $\text{CH}_3$) plus 4 distinct ring carbons only if it is para disubstituted, because the two sides of the ring are symmetric. An ortho or meta isomer would make all 6 ring carbons inequivalent and give up to 8 peaks. So the $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COCH}_3$ groups must be para to each other. Hence A is 4-hydroxyacetophenone: $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-CH}_3$ (para).

Draw B and the iodoform pair C + D**
Bromination puts Br in both ortho positions to the activating $\text{OH}$, so B is 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxyacetophenone. For the iodoform reaction: $$\text{R-CO-CH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-COO}^- + \text{CHI}_3 + 3\text{I}^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ side chain is cleaved. The yellow precipitate C is triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_3$. The remaining fragment R becomes the carboxylate, shown as the acid D: 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}$ (para). Note the carbon count drops from $\text{C}_8$ in A to $\text{C}_7$ in D plus one carbon in $\text{CHI}_3$, which balances.

Convert the acid D to the acyl chloride E**
Carboxylic acids react with $\text{PCl}_5$ to give acyl chlorides: $$\text{R-COOH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{R-COCl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$$ So D, $\text{C}_7\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$, loses $\text{OH}$ and gains $\text{Cl}$ to give E, $\text{C}_7\text{H}_5\text{O}_2\text{Cl}$. That is 4-hydroxybenzoyl chloride, $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCl}$ (para). In this scheme the phenolic $\text{OH}$ is retained in the drawn product.

Form the ester F**
Acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols to form esters: $$\text{R-COCl} + \text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHOH} \rightarrow \text{R-COOCH(CH}_3)_2 + \text{HCl}$$ With propan-2-ol, $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CHOH}$, you get the isopropyl ester. So F is isopropyl 4-hydroxybenzoate, $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COO-CH(CH}_3)_2$ (para).

Final answer: A: $p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$, 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethan-1-one, OH para to $\text{COCH}_3$.
B: 3,5-dibromo derivative, $p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_2\text{COCH}_3$ with Br ortho to OH on both sides.
C: $\text{CHI}_3$, triiodomethane.
D: $p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COOH}$, 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, OH para to COOH.
E: $p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCl}$, 4-hydroxybenzoyl chloride, OH para to COCl.
F: $p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$, isopropyl 4-hydroxybenzoate.
